name: Teetsh
tagline: Web app where teachers build lesson plans, worksheets, timetables and class records from curriculum-aligned templates.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The mechanical core here is a structured document editor with print-ready layouts, a class roster, and a weekly timetable grid. An agent can produce that in a weekend: SQLite, a block editor, a print stylesheet that actually respects A4 margins. What it cannot produce is the pre-loaded curriculum reference for a specific national school system, the template library other teachers already filled, or the confidence that a worksheet prints correctly the first time at 7am. Teachers are the least patient software users on earth because their deadline is a room of thirty children. A personal build works if you are willing to type your own curriculum objectives once and accept that print CSS will fight you.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you keep classes, students and a weekly timetable, then write lesson plans and worksheets from reusable templates and print them to clean A4 PDFs.
requirements: Willingness to enter your own curriculum objectives and template text
whatYouLose: Curriculum objectives pre-loaded and tagged for your country's official programme
The shared library of templates and resources other teachers already made
Layouts that have been debugged against real printers, not just Chrome's preview
Any mobile or tablet experience worth using in a classroom
Sync across school laptop, home laptop and phone unless you wire up your own hosting
moatNotes: The curriculum mapping and the accumulated template corpus are the asset. The editor is table stakes.
whyPeopleStillPay: Teachers pay for time, not features. A tool that already knows the official programme structure, already has a worksheet layout that prints correctly, and already contains something close to the lesson you need saves hours every Sunday evening. Your own build gives you the editor but hands you back the data entry, which is exactly the work you wanted to avoid. If you teach one subject to one age group and reuse the same six document types, the trade is fine. If you need breadth, it is not.
notes: Print CSS is the real boss fight, not the editor.
prompt:
Build a local-first lesson planning app for a single teacher. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, schema created on first run, file at ./data/teetsh.db
- Tailwind CSS
- No auth, no external APIs, no analytics

Data model:
- classes: name, school year, level label
- students: name, class id, notes
- subjects: name, color
- objectives: subject id, code, text (user entered, this is the curriculum reference)
- templates: name, subject id, JSON block structure
- documents: title, class id, subject id, date, linked objective ids, JSON blocks, created from template id
- timetable_slots: class id, weekday, start time, end time, subject id, label

Features in scope:
1. CRUD for classes, students, subjects, objectives.
2. Weekly timetable: a grid, weekday columns, 30 minute rows, click to add or edit a slot, drag not required.
3. Document editor: an ordered list of blocks. Block types: heading, rich text (plain textarea with markdown rendering is fine), bullet list, table with editable rows and columns, image from local file copied into ./data/uploads, page break. Add, delete, reorder blocks with up and down buttons.
4. Save any document as a template, create a new document from a template.
5. Print view at /documents/[id]/print with a dedicated print stylesheet: A4, 15mm margins, no nav, no buttons, respects page breaks, header with class name and date. This must actually look right in Chrome print preview. Spend real effort here.
6. Search documents by title, subject and class.

Out of scope: sharing, multi user, PDF generation libraries (browser print only), mobile layout beyond not being broken, any curriculum data shipped by you.

Seed the database with two example subjects, one class with five students, one template and one document so the app is not empty on first run.

Add a README with setup commands and one paragraph explaining that objectives must be entered manually because official curriculum text is not bundled.
